rv.q: It’s an utterly disarming evening that shows happiness as a day-to-day mindset, not a far-off dream.
Marvellous is the perfect argument for a welcoming theatre space.
Marvellous answers the warm embrace of the theatre with a markedly communal form of entertainment that feels like a much-needed hug.
'Marvellous' is both a perfect fit for this freshly minted venue, and a lively affirmation of the power of thinking differently.
And to launch a new venue not with a star vehicle but with a joyous show, delivered by a neurodiverse cast, that celebrates the potential in difference, well, that’s quite marvellous.
Like its subject, this playful, exuberant theatrical happening wins you over with sheer heart and good humour.
It’s all quite sentimental, like Alan Bennett without the acid, and the slapstick is sometimes slapdash.
Baldwin’s story could make a great play – but this isn’t it.
This is surely a venue with lots of exciting programming in the pipeline (beyond what has already been revealed) – happily starting with its best foot forwards.

Its optimistic warmth makes Marvellous an audience-friendly opener for Nimax’s new theatre and this transfer from an in-the-round provincial theatre demonstrates the possibilities it provides for the future with its ability to change its configuration.
An excellent cast of seven actors share the storytelling, led by Michael Hugo in a strong performance as “the real Neil”.
The show is a list of actions which don’t add up to a drama.
But as a celebration of an eccentric character whose struggles have a wider resonance, this works very well.

But you can’t help but feel more sophisticated storytelling would allow Marvellous to live up to its name and draw in those spectators – and London will be full of them – new to the happiness Neil imparted, and who might like that quality fully dramatised and not just larkily announced.
This slice of pure theatre joy really is Marvellous.
It is just a bit of silly fun, an audacious move in its lack of audaciousness.
The thing is that it’s a delightful show featuring a brilliant and much original narrative of a wowing real life, able to move and generate a good bunch of emotions (and reflections) at many levels.

cn.t: Critics find this heartwarming bio-drama about Neil Baldwin a charming, life-affirming opener for the new @sohoplace theatre, praising its sincerity and exuberance, though some question whether the modest production matches the venue's ambition.
